extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (prosecutors/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the USPTO two-step (Alice/Mayo) subject-matter eligibility analysis for patent claims, including Step 1 statutory-category check, Step 2A (directed to a judicial exception) and Step 2B (significantly more), plus procedural form-paragraph requirements for §101 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (the four statutory categories). If the claim is not directed to one of these statutory categories, reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This step has not changed and is explained in MPEP 2106(I). Use revised form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 for such rejections and continue examination for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions). "Directed to" means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no (not directed to an exception), the claim is eligible and examination should continue for patentability. Examples of concepts courts have found to be exceptions are provided in Parts I.A.2 and IV of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use streamlined analysis when claim does not 'tie up' an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim when viewed as a whole clearly does not seek to 'tie up' any judicial exception, use the "streamlined analysis" discussed in Part I.B.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamlined analysis applies where a claim clearly does not preempt or monopolize the exception; see the referenced part for procedures and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a nature-based product limitation, use the markedly different characteristics analysis to evaluate whether the claim is directed to a 'product of nature' that falls under the law of nature/natural phenomenon exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine whether this analysis is needed and how to perform it, see Part I.A.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. For products of nature, explain how the characteristics are not markedly different from the product’s naturally occurring counterpart (example given: a naturally occurring DNA segment that conveys the same genetic information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' (additional elements analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception. If no, the claim is ineligible; if yes, the claim is eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional elements should be considered both individually and as an ordered combination (elements that do not appear to add significantly more individually may do so in combination). The Supreme Court has identified considerations for determining whether additional elements amount to significantly more; examples and applications are in Parts I.B.1 and III of the Interim Eligibility Guidance. Examination should continue for patentability in either case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate each claim separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider each claim separately based on the particular elements recited therein — claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform the eligibility analysis claim-by-claim; do not assume the outcome for one claim dictates the outcome for another even if similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling claims directed to multiple exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a plurality of exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in a claim. Conversely, if the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible and no further eligibility analysis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.05 — §101 rejection heading and procedural placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.05 is the §101 rejection heading to be used when rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner note: (1) This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.04.01 in first actions and final rejections. (2) It must be followed by a detailed explanation of the grounds of rejection using one or more specific form paragraphs (7.05.01, 7.05.015, 7.05.02, 7.05.03, or another appropriate reason). See MPEP §§ 706.03(a) and 2105 - 2107.03 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.05.01 — rejection for non-statutory (not one of the four categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph 7.05.01 when the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter because it does not fall within at least one of the four categories of patent eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner note: (1) Should be preceded by 7.05. (2) In the bracket, explain why the claimed invention is not patent eligible by identifying what the claim is directed to and explain why it does not fall within at least one of the four categories (examples: signal per se, mere information in the form of data, a contract between two parties, or a human being). (3) For a claim directed to a judicial exception and non-statutory, use form paragraph 7.05.015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.05.015 — rejection for judicial exception without 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph 7.05.015 when the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea) without significantly more. The template requires identifying the claim(s), identifying the exception as recited in the claim, and explaining why the claim(s) do not include additional elements sufficient to amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner notes provide detailed bracket guidance: (3) identify the claim(s) that recite the exception; (4) in bracket 2 identify and explain how the exception is recited in the claim and why it is an exception (examples: 'Arrhenius equation' or 'series of steps instructing how to hedge risk'); for products of nature explain lack of markedly different characteristics (example: naturally occurring DNA segment conveying same genetic information); (5) in bracket 3 identify additional elements and explain why, separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more (examples: generically recited computer elements that would be routine in any computer implementation; routine data gathering steps used to apply a correlation). This form is for use with all claim types and any judicial exception.
